lesson.subject: anatomy
lesson.title: Midgut herniation, rotation and fixation
lesson.summary: The standard model describes an initial 90-degree rotation during physiological herniation and a further 180 degrees during return.

steps.title: Midgut Herniation and Rotation
steps.body: The midgut elongates rapidly, forms a primary intestinal loop, temporarily herniates into the umbilical cord, rotates around the superior mesenteric artery, and later returns to the abdomen.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Physiologic umbilical herniation occurs because the midgut grows faster than the early abdominal cavity. Total rotation is classically described as 270 degrees counterclockwise around SMA when viewed from the front. Cecal bud initially lies high and later descends toward the right iliac fossa. Errors can cause malrotation, volvulus risk, nonrotation, reversed rotation, or abnormal fixation.

steps.title: Why does abnormal fixation matter even after bowel has returned to the abdomen?
steps.body: Return and rotation place bowel in a general arrangement, but mesenteric fixation determines how broad and stable its attachment becomes. A narrow mesenteric base can allow bowel and vessels to twist together, threatening perfusion. The cecum normally migrates from a relatively high position toward the right iliac region, while different mesenteries remain mobile or fuse. These later spatial events mean that being inside the abdominal cavity is not enough to establish normal rotational and fixation anatomy.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The standard model describes an initial 90-degree rotation during physiological herniation and a further 180 degrees during return. State the viewing direction because reversing the view reverses apparent clockwise movement. After return, the cecum descends and mesenteries fix selectively. A narrow mesenteric attachment in malrotation permits twisting of bowel and its vessels. Normal temporary herniation is not the same as persistence of bowel outside the abdominal cavity after the expected return.
